Call or Text  (424) 435-2326


Last updated November 14, 2026.

Who bills Phoenix property tax

Maricopa County bills it, not the city. The Maricopa County Assessor decides each parcel's value and classification. Billing and collection fall to the Maricopa County Treasurer, who takes in money for more than 1,800 tax districts (state, county, cities and towns, schools, community colleges and special districts) and distributes it.

So a Phoenix owner calls one of two offices, depending on the question.

  • Assessor: what your Notice of Valuation says, your home's legal class, appeals, notices of claim and personal exemptions. Visit 301 W Jefferson St, Phoenix, AZ 85003, or use the appeals line, 602-506-3406.
  • Treasurer: what you owe, how to pay, refunds, delinquent notices and tax lien questions.

The city picks its own rates yet never assesses your home or takes your payment. What it levies is one line among the others on your county bill.

Due dates and penalties

Payment is split between October 1 and the next March 1 (A.R.S. 42-18052). Delinquency begins after 5:00 p.m. on November 1 for the first half and May 1 for the second, and a weekend or holiday pushes that to 5:00 p.m. the next business day.

This year it applied. With November 1 on a Sunday, 2026's first half went delinquent after 5 p.m. Monday, November 2, so any unpaid first half is late now. Next spring, May 1, 2027 lands on a Saturday and the second-half deadline should roll to Monday, May 3, 2027.

Interest on late tax is simple, 16 percent annually, and any part of a month is billed as a full month (A.R.S. 42-18053). Pay the entire year by December 31 and none is collected. If you haven't paid your 2026 first half, you therefore have until Thursday, December 31, 2026 to pay both halves clean. Small bills of $100 or less are due in one piece on October 1 and go delinquent after December 31.

Payment or noticeDate or rule
First half dueOctober 1
First half delinquent, 2026After 5 p.m. on Monday, November 2, 2026
Final delinquent notices for unpaid 2025 taxDecember 1
Full year without interestDecember 31, 2026
Second half dueMarch 1, 2027

Phoenix housing and tax districts

Phoenix had an estimated 1,665,481 residents in July 2025. Among the city's 15 urban villages are Ahwatukee Foothills, Camelback East, Laveen, Maryvale, Encanto and South Mountain. Owners occupy 57.3 percent of homes, and the median owner-occupied home is valued at $420,700.

Housing varies a great deal within city limits, and the school, community college and special districts on your bill follow the parcel. Homes in Maryvale and Ahwatukee Foothills share a city without sharing a bill. The Assessor's site shows which districts cover your address; houses only a mile apart may carry different total rates.

What the city itself charges

The city's published notice for 2026-27 proposed a primary rate of $1.2652 per $100 of assessed valuation, slightly down from $1.2658, and a secondary rate of $0.7745, down from $0.8141. The city said that even with the lower primary rate, rising assessed values would still lift primary taxes for the average owner by 2.79 percent. Ask the Treasurer which rates are in effect.

Primary and secondary tax pay for different things.

  • Primary tax supports General Fund services such as police and fire, parks and recreation, libraries and community centers. State law limits how fast a city's primary levy can grow (A.R.S. 42-17051).
  • Secondary tax pays bonded debt service for facilities such as libraries, police and fire stations, storm drains and parks.

That covers just the city. County, school district and community college rates are added on top, so the full bill exceeds the city's line. Maricopa County posts rate and levy tables for every taxing jurisdiction on its Tax Levy and Rates page.

Challenging your home valuation

File with the Maricopa County Assessor no more than 60 days after the mailing date of your Notice of Valuation (A.R.S. 42-16051). Late winter is when notices arrive. Find the mail date printed on yours and count forward 60 days.

Three different filings are described on the Assessor's appeals page. Picking the wrong one wastes time.

  • Real property appeal: use it if you think full cash value or classification is incorrect. The Petition for Review of Valuation (AZDOR Form 82130R) goes in by mail or in person, and emailed appeals aren't accepted.
  • Notice of Claim: use it when the record has a plain error, such as the wrong square footage. It looks back over this year and three earlier ones, and an approved claim may bring a refund via the Treasurer.
  • Residential Legal Class Change: use it once a home becomes your primary residence. You'll need documents showing your name at the property address, namely a driver's license, voter registration, or a tax return address page paired with a vehicle registration or utility bill.

Attach evidence to any of them. An appeal lacking appraisals, comparable sales or similar documents can be denied.

Homeowner exemptions

Personal exemptions for widowed, totally disabled and veteran owners come from the Assessor's Valuation Relief division. February 28 is the application deadline, extended to September 1 for those with an approved Exemption Deadline Waiver. All of them require Arizona residency and household income below the statutory limit.

  • Widowed or totally disabled: up to $4,873 off the limited property value.
  • Veteran with a service-connected disability under 100 percent, or a nonservice-connected disability: up to $4,873, multiplied by the disability percentage.
  • Veteran with a 100 percent service-connected rating: the primary residence is fully exempt when every requirement, income included, is met.

The income cap is $39,865 for households with no children under 18, and $47,826 where children under 18 or disabled children lived in the home the prior year. Social Security, military pensions and VA disability payments don't count as income. Call 602-506-3406 before applying, because buying or selling property can end eligibility.

Selling with unpaid taxes

Plan to settle back taxes by closing at the latest. Under A.R.S. 42-18104, a county treasurer may sell one lien covering every delinquent year on the property. The title company can pull the balance and list it on the settlement statement.

A few steps keep closing on schedule.

  • Request a payoff figure from the escrow officer, with interest counted to the closing date.
  • An open first half for 2026 has been accruing interest from November 2.
  • Paid off a mortgage recently? The Treasurer can explain the waiver in A.R.S. 42-18053(C): it applies to a delinquency within a year of a mortgage or deed of trust release, requires board of supervisors approval, and works once per property.

Your deed is filed with the Maricopa County Recorder, whose staff won't give legal advice, fill in documents or notarize. Reach recording services at 602-506-3535. The steps are identical for a cash buyer or a financed one.

Frequently asked questions

Does Phoenix itself collect my property tax?

No. Maricopa County's Treasurer bills and collects it, including the city's portion, and the Assessor sets your value. The city's rate is one line on that bill.

What is the last day to pay 2026 Phoenix property tax without interest?

December 31, 2026, covering the full year. A.R.S. 42-18053 waives interest on a full-year payment made by December 31 of the tax year. Paying only the first half after November 2 leaves interest running on what's unpaid.

What interest rate hits late Maricopa County property tax?

Sixteen percent annually, simple, from the delinquency date until paid, with part of a month counted whole. After a mortgage release, the treasurer may waive interest once per property if the board approves.

Can I still appeal my Phoenix home value?

Yes, if you file within 60 days of the mail date on your Notice of Valuation. For a plain factual error, such as wrong square footage, a Notice of Claim can reach back three prior tax years.

Do I have to pay Phoenix property tax before I sell?

Clear it at or before closing, with interest in the payoff. Your title officer or the Maricopa County Treasurer can give the exact amount for your parcel.

Cash Home Buyers in Arizona
Cash Offer in 24 Hours

  • No fees, commissions or closing costs on a Tucson, AZ Property Tax Guide sale

Owe Tucson Property Tax? Get a Cash Offer

Call or Text  (424) 435-2326


Last updated November 14, 2026.

Behind on Tucson property tax?

Who bills property tax in Tucson

A single county statement covers everything. For a Tucson house, the Pima County Treasurer sends the bill and takes payment, while the Pima County Assessor decides the value. The city's own levy rides on that same statement, so there is no separate city bill.

Two offices answer most questions:

  • Pima County Assessor, 240 N. Stone Avenue, Tucson, AZ 85701, 520-724-8630: valuation, classification, notices of value, appeals and exemptions
  • Pima County Treasurer, 520-724-8341: statements, payments, delinquency and lien redemption

Tucson has 228,020 households, and 51.8% are owner-occupied, so just under half rent. Landlords and owner-occupants receive the same county bill.

Due dates for 2026 and 2027

The yearly bill splits into two parts. Part one is due October 1 and goes late after 5 p.m. on November 1; part two is due March 1 and goes late after 5 p.m. on May 1. If a late date lands on a weekend or holiday, it shifts to 5 p.m. the next business day.

Payment step2026 tax year date
First half dueOctober 1, 2026
Full-year payment, first-half interest waivedBefore 5 p.m. December 31, 2026
Second half dueMarch 1, 2027
Second half postmark deadlineMay 3, 2027

A bill of $100 or less is due in full with the first installment. Is the 2026 first half still open? Call the Treasurer for the balance now owed. Interest on the first half is waived only when the whole year is paid or postmarked before 5 p.m. on December 31.

The city rate and your combined rate

The City Manager's recommended budget for fiscal year 2027 proposes a primary property tax rate of $0.4245 per $100 of assessed valuation, which is $0.0208 below the FY26 rate. The drop comes mostly from a smaller tort liability claim in the levy, from $1,733,290 to $989,850. The levy stays within 2% above the prior year's maximum allowable levy, plus new construction, as the state constitution allows.

The city rate makes up just one slice. Your tax is assessed value multiplied by a total rate that combines the city, county, schools and special districts. Your Pima County statement shows the combined rate that applies in your tax area.

Free, no-obligation offerTell us about your house and get a written cash offer within 24 hours.Get My Cash Offer →

How to pay and what it costs

Payment options are online, in person, by mail and by wire. The online portal takes most debit and credit cards, PayPal and eCheck, and charges a convenience fee.

  • eCheck: $0.50 per transaction
  • Cards and other digital wallets online: 1.95% of the payment, with a $1.95 minimum
  • In person at the Pima County Public Service Center: card, cash, check, cashier's check or money order, with a 2% fee on card payments
  • By mail: a check, cashier's check or money order in US funds, made out to the Pima County Treasurer. Never mail cash.
  • Returned items: $25.00 charge

The post office does not always postmark mail, so mail early or get a receipt. Bank wires are arranged through the office at 520-724-8341. If a lender pays your taxes, ask them to confirm each payment. To change a mailing address, use the Assessor, which requires a notarized form unless you update it online on the parcel record.

How to appeal your valuation

Your window is 60 days from the postmark on the Notice of Value, and the petition goes to the Pima County Assessor. Notices are mailed by March 1. What you can challenge is the valuation or classification; a big tax bill is not itself a ground.

Pima County has four appeal tracks:

  • Petition: 60 days from the postmark of a Notice of Value mailed by March 1
  • Supplemental: 25 days after a Notice of Change mailed on or before September 30
  • Notice of Proposed Correction: 60 days, when the Assessor starts a correction at any time of year
  • Notice of Claim: an owner-started appeal for factual errors in the record

Pick a valuation method and name it. Under a market approach you cite a comparable sale nearby, or a sale of your own property. Your case is stronger if the record has wrong details, if full cash value exceeds similar homes or sales in the last three years, or if the limited property value was calculated incorrectly.

Every appeal gets a ruling from the Assessor by August 15. Unhappy owners then have 25 calendar days to take it to the State Board of Equalization, which rules by October 15, and 60 days after the last administrative decision to reach Tax Court. Skipping the administrative steps is allowed: go straight to Tax Court by December 15 of the valuation year.

Exemptions and relief programs

Exemptions exist for disabled military service members, widows, widowers and people with a total and permanent disability, along with a valuation freeze for seniors. The Pima County Assessor administers them, and the Valuation Relief Team can be reached at 520-724-7500 or ASRValRelief@pima.gov.

  • A 100% service-connected disabled veteran can receive an exemption on one primary residence, effective for tax year 2026 and after under H.B. 2792. The applicant needs an honorable discharge, a VA benefit summary letter and income under the limits.
  • The income cap is $34,901 with no children under 18 at home, or $41,870 if a qualifying child lives there.
  • File a new exemption application with the Assessor between the first Monday in January and March 1.
  • The Senior Freeze, formally the Property Valuation Protection Option, fixes a primary residence's valuation for a renewable three-year period for owners who meet age and income limits.
  • Widow, widower and total and permanent disability exemptions cover a set dollar amount, with assessed value and income limits.

When a surviving spouse sells a home that carries the veteran's exemption, the exemption ends with the sale.

Selling with taxes owed

Whatever you still owe comes out of your sale proceeds when you close. Have your title company request a payoff figure from the Pima County Treasurer that matches the closing date, since interest may add to a past-due balance.

Pima County also allows a person who owns an interest in the property, an agent, an assignee or an attorney to redeem a sold tax lien in full, and any person may pay on the owner's behalf as a charitable gift. The Treasurer's office can tell you who qualifies to redeem and what proof is needed.

Selling for cash? Disclose any delinquent installment right away. A house with a past-due 2026 first half can still close, since escrow pays the balance and records the deed with an Affidavit of Property Value. Get the payoff in writing and compare it with the figure on your latest statement.

Frequently asked questions

Does the City of Tucson send a separate property tax bill?

No. The Pima County Treasurer bills all property tax, including the City of Tucson levy, on one statement. The City Manager's recommended FY27 primary rate is $0.4245 per $100 of assessed valuation.

When is the second half of Tucson property tax due?

The due date is March 1, 2027, with delinquency after 5 p.m. on May 1. The postmark deadline for the 2026 second half is May 3, 2027.

What happens if my first-half tax is late?

Interest applies to the late first half. A full-year payment made before 5 p.m. on December 31, 2026 removes interest on that installment. Call the Treasurer at 520-724-8341 for the exact balance.

How do I appeal my Tucson property value?

Petition the Pima County Assessor within 60 days of the Notice of Value postmark; notices go out by March 1. A ruling is due by August 15, after which you get 25 calendar days to go to the State Board of Equalization.

Is there a property tax exemption for a disabled veteran in Tucson?

Yes. A veteran with a 100% service-connected disability rating can apply to the Pima County Assessor for an exemption on one primary residence for tax year 2026 and later, subject to income limits. Call 520-724-7500 for the Valuation Relief Team.

Cash Home Buyers in Arizona
Cash Offer in 24 Hours
  • Yuma, AZ Property Tax Guide: inherited, behind on payments, tenants or repairs, we buy the house as-is
  • No fees, commissions or closing costs on a Yuma, AZ Property Tax Guide sale
  • Turn the Yuma, AZ Property Tax Guide offer down and you owe us nothing

Owe Yuma Property Tax? Get a Cash Offer

We buy Yuma houses as-is.

Call or Text  (424) 435-2326


Last updated November 14, 2026.

Behind on Yuma property tax?
We buy Yuma houses as-is, and the title company pays unpaid tax from the proceeds.
Get My Cash Offer →

Who bills property tax in Yuma

If you own a home inside Yuma city limits, the Yuma County Treasurer sends your tax bill and collects payment, and the Yuma County Assessor decides what the property is worth. You will find both under one roof in the county seat, 197 S. Main Street, Yuma, AZ 85364. Suite 203 holds the Treasurer's counter.

For billing questions, call the Treasurer at (928) 539-7781 or write to treasury@yumacountyaz.gov. Payment choices include:

  • Scanning the QR code printed on the payment coupon
  • Paying online at yumacountyaz.gov/paytaxes
  • Using the phone line at 1-877-690-3729 and jurisdiction code 1311
  • Mailing a check or using bank bill pay to Yuma County Treasurer, 197 S. Main St., Suite 203

Certified funds are required for delinquent 2024 taxes. For assessment questions, the Assessor's number is (928) 373-6040 and the email is assr-info@yumacountyaz.gov. Look up owner names, parcel details and sales data on the Assessor's online records site; it takes the place of the old ITAX property tax site.

Property tax due dates

The county uses the statewide schedule. October 1 and March 1 are the due dates, and a half becomes delinquent once 5:00 p.m. passes on the next November 1 or May 1. A weekend date moves to the next business day, hence the specific 2026 and 2027 dates in this list.

DateTax event
October 1, 20262026 first-half installment due
December 31, 2026Last day to pay all of 2026 with no interest
January 1, 20275% penalty added to delinquent 2025 taxes
February 17, 2027, 5:00 p.m.Deadline to pay 2025 taxes and stay out of the lien sale
February 18, 2027Lien sale for unpaid 2025 taxes
March 1, 20272026 second-half installment due
May 3, 2027, 5:00 p.m.Second half becomes delinquent

Tax statements go out in September each year, and the county mails delinquent notices in mid-May. File the notice with your closing papers. It shows the parcel number and amount the title company will ask for. An unpaid first half of 2026 calls for a quick phone call to the Treasurer to learn the balance.

What the City of Yuma adds

The city levies a primary property tax of its own, and it must announce increases in public under A.R.S. 42-17107. For the current cycle the City of Yuma proposed raising primary property taxes by $431,353, or 2.51 percent, over the prior year.

Its council gathers in Council Chambers on the first and third Wednesday of each month at 5:30 p.m. at City Hall, One City Plaza. Your total depends on the district codes attached to your parcel. The Yuma County Treasurer can itemize each jurisdiction on it.

Free, no-obligation offerTell us about your house and get a written cash offer within 24 hours.Get My Cash Offer →

How to challenge your valuation

Your appeal goes to the Assessor and must arrive within 60 days of the mailing date on the Notice of Value. Your exact deadline appears on the card, mailed each winter. A card that never shows up still starts the clock, so phone the office if yours is missing.

Before you appeal, read the Notice of Value closely. It lists Full Cash Value and Limited Property Value, and the back explains the legal class codes.

  • Code 3.01 means an owner-occupied primary residence. Owners with that code already receive the Less State Aid to Education reduction from the Treasurer.
  • Code 4.02 marks a rental. If the classification is wrong, the Assessor wants proof that you live in the home more than nine months a year.
  • Acceptable proof includes an Arizona driver's license, Arizona ID card, voter card or state income tax return, along with the Affidavit of Primary Residence.

Appeals to tax court end on December 15.

Relief programs for homeowners

Three programs run through the Assessor.

  • Widow, widower and disability exemption. It also covers churches and certain non-profit organizations. The filing period runs from the first working day in January to March 1, and the Assessor offers the current guidelines and a physician's Certification of Disability form.
  • Senior Property Valuation Protection Option. Known as the Senior Freeze, this one can be filed from January 1 to September 1.
  • Veteran exemption. It falls under A.R.S. 42-11111, as changed by House Bill 4168. The first tax year it covers is 2027, and the Assessor opens applications January 4, 2027. A one-page flyer on the Assessor's page explains who qualifies.

Bring identification and ask the Assessor what proof applies to your situation before you file. If you are about to sell, remember that these benefits attach to the current owner. The buyer will need to apply on their own once they hold the deed, so mention it when you hand over the house.

Selling with taxes owed

Taxes you owe follow the house, so escrow usually pays them out of the seller's proceeds. Under A.R.S. 42-17153, each tax year's lien is created on January 1. It outranks most other liens, with two exceptions: state liens and liens for taxes of other years. Buyers and lenders expect it to be cleared.

Late tax earns simple interest at 16 percent a year under A.R.S. 42-18053; pay the whole year by December 31 and no interest applies. A 5 percent penalty hits delinquent 2025 taxes on January 1, 2027, and a tax lien sale follows in February. The Board of Supervisors Auditorium, 197 S Main St., hosts the sale: registration opens at 8:00 a.m. and bidding starts at 9:00 a.m.

Request a current payoff on your parcel from the Treasurer ahead of signing any contract. Late years cost more each month, so the earlier you know the figure, the more room you have to negotiate. At closing the title company deducts the tax owed, divides the current year between you and the buyer, and sends the payment to the county, so you do not need to visit the Treasurer yourself. Selling for cash? Mention any balance in your first conversation, and have the title company confirm the figure in writing.

A simple order of work keeps a sale on track. First, find your latest tax notice and confirm both halves are paid or scheduled. Second, give the parcel number to your title company when the contract is signed. Third, review the payoff it returns a few days before closing, because interest changes the figure from week to week. Last, keep your receipts in case a lender or the buyer asks to see proof of payment. A seller who moves out before the bill arrives should leave a forwarding address with the Treasurer so notices do not get lost.

Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

Yuma context for homeowners

Yuma lies in Arizona's southwest corner along the Colorado River and had 95,548 residents at the 2020 census. Winter vegetable farming and the military drive the economy. About 117 days a year reach 100 degrees or more, which wears roofs, cooling systems and exterior paint, so get a quote for anything near the end of its life before you list.

Most of the city lies in the Yuma Union High School District, with central and eastern Yuma in Yuma Elementary District One and the northwest in the Crane district.

Frequently asked questions

When is Yuma property tax due?

The bill splits in two, due October 1 and March 1. A half is late once 5:00 p.m. passes on the next November 1 or May 1, moved for weekends. For 2026 taxes the second half is due March 1, 2027, with the late date set at 5:00 p.m. on May 3, 2027. Nothing accrues if the entire year is settled by December 31.

Who do I call about my Yuma property tax bill?

Call the Yuma County Treasurer at (928) 539-7781 or write to treasury@yumacountyaz.gov for billing and payment questions. For value and classification questions, call the Yuma County Assessor at (928) 373-6040 or email assr-info@yumacountyaz.gov. Both offices are at 197 S. Main Street in Yuma.

How long do I have to appeal my Yuma property value?

Sixty days from the mailing date of the Notice of Value, and the card prints your exact deadline. A tax court appeal cannot be filed after December 15.

Does the City of Yuma charge its own property tax?

Yes, a primary tax, and the city proposed a 2.51 percent increase of $431,353 for the current cycle. The Yuma County Treasurer can give you the jurisdiction breakdown for your parcel.

What penalty applies to late Yuma County property tax?

Simple interest of 16 percent a year starts at delinquency (A.R.S. 42-18053). On January 1, 2027, delinquent 2025 taxes add a 5 percent penalty, and the tax lien sale is February 18, 2027.

Get My Cash Offer →

Who bills property tax in Scottsdale

Scottsdale itself mails no property tax bill. Maricopa County does the billing: its Assessor sets the value, and its Treasurer mails the bill and takes the payment. Scottsdale adds its own rate to that same county bill, next to the school district, fire and other districts on your parcel.

The city's 2025/26 property tax rate is $0.4891 primary and $0.4233 secondary, $0.9124 combined, per $100 of assessed valuation. The primary share covers everyday city operations, while the secondary share retires debt on voter-approved bonds. Rates for 2026/27 may differ, so read the rate lines on your own bill.

Scottsdale had an estimated 243,006 residents on July 1, 2025. Homes there have a median owner-occupied value of $789,800 for 2020 to 2024, and owners occupy 67.0 percent of the housing. Parcels near the city line can fall under a neighbor such as Phoenix, Paradise Valley, Carefree, Fountain Hills or Tempe, so confirm the city and districts printed on your bill.

Due dates and deadlines

The bill is split into halves. October 1 is the first half's due date. Half two arrives March 1, 2027, and becomes late when 5 p.m. on May 1, 2027 passes. Settle the full year by December 31 and half one is interest-free. December 1 is when final delinquent notices are sent.

A bill that totals $100 or less goes late at 5 p.m. on December 31. Overdue tax earns simple interest of 16 percent a year. ARS 42-18053 adds a one-time relief: if the board approves, the treasurer can waive interest and penalties on a delinquency that follows within a year of a mortgage or deed of trust being released. Each property can use it once.

EventDate or rule
First halfDue October 1
Second halfDue March 1; late after 5 p.m. on May 1
Full year without interestPaid by 5 p.m. December 31, for bills over $100
Valuation appealSixty days from the date the Notice of Value goes out
Assessor's answerOn or before August 15
Court appealFiled by December 15 of that notice year

Why a high value doesn't mean a high bill

What the county taxes is the limited property value. Growth in that figure is held to 5 percent a year, with exceptions for new construction, a significant change to the property or a change of use. A big appraisal number therefore doesn't automatically mean a big bill. When a buyer asks about taxes, point to the actual figures on your own bill.

Owners near the McDowell Sonoran Preserve or the Indian Bend Wash Greenbelt should check parcel data for flood and preserve boundaries before listing. Buyers tend to ask about both.

How to appeal a Scottsdale valuation

Home owners file Form 82130R, the Petition for Review of Valuation, with the Maricopa County Assessor. Sixty days from the date of the Notice of Value is the cutoff, and the Assessor sends notices by March 1. Visit 301 W Jefferson St, Phoenix, AZ 85003, or call 602-506-3406. Appeals sent by email are refused. A petition with no documents behind it, such as comparable sales or an appraisal, may be denied.

Two items are open to appeal: full cash value and legal class. The limited property value, which actually sets your tax, is off the table. Expect the Assessor's answer by August 15. Disagree with it and you get 25 days to take the matter to the State Board of Equalization, the body that hears these cases for Maricopa County and issues decisions by mid-October. The final route is court, either tax court or small claims, filed by December 15 of the notice year or inside 60 days of the last administrative ruling. Small claims can hear appeals on owner-occupied homes and on property valued under $2 million. The tax court line is 602-506-8297.

  • A Notice of Claim fits a factual mistake, such as the wrong square footage or year built. It can reach the current year and the three tax years before it, and it may produce a refund.
  • Use the Residential Legal Class Change form if the house recently became your primary residence. A change made between January 1 and July 1 can fix both the current and next tax year.

A new owner of property whose value or class the former owner never appealed may file in court before December 15 of the year the taxes are levied.

What happens if taxes go unpaid

Maricopa County secures unpaid taxes by selling liens, as ARS 42-18101 directs, through an online auction vendor. The lien is a claim for the tax. You still own the house, but the lien has to be paid with interest to clear it. Tax lien staff at the Treasurer take calls at 602-506-8511.

If a lien or open balance is on the parcel, tell the title company before you sign a contract. It will want the payoff included in the closing figures.

Short-term rentals and legal class

Scottsdale charges a 5.0 percent transient lodging tax on stays of 29 days or less, on top of its 1.7 percent privilege tax. Neither is part of the property bill. A house used for guests may also carry a different legal class on the county roll, so ask the Assessor how yours is classified before listing.

Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

Selling a Scottsdale house with taxes owed

  • Look up the parcel on the Treasurer's website and write down every balance, earlier years included.
  • Have the Treasurer quote a payoff with interest through the day you close.
  • Ask the Assessor about legal class, exemptions and the mailing address before the sale.
  • Give the payoff figures to the title or escrow company handling your closing.

Exemptions are another thing to check. Under ARS 42-11111, exemptions reach widows, widowers, owners with a total and permanent disability, and disabled former service members. Passing title to the buyer ends the exemption on that house. The Assessor can tell you which ones apply to you. A cash sale changes none of this. The buyer still takes title with the taxes settled, and the payoff comes out of your proceeds. For a smooth closing, gather three things ahead of time: the payoff figures, a note of whether an appeal or Notice of Claim is pending, and the legal class the Assessor has on file for the house.

Frequently asked questions

Who do I pay property tax to in Scottsdale?

Payment goes to the Maricopa County Treasurer, while the county Assessor sets the value. The city's rate rides along on the county bill, which means a single bill and a single payment.

When is the next Scottsdale property tax due date?

March 1, 2027 is the due date for the second half, and it is delinquent after 5 p.m. on May 1, 2027. A full-year payment by December 31 spares the first half from interest.

What is the Scottsdale city property tax rate?

For 2025/26 the city rate is $0.4891 primary and $0.4233 secondary, $0.9124 combined, per $100 of assessed valuation. Your bill also carries school, fire and county rates, and 2026/27 figures may differ.

What if I missed the 60 day appeal deadline in Scottsdale?

A Notice of Claim can still fix a factual error for the current year and three earlier years. The next appeal window opens when the Assessor mails notices by March 1.

Does a new owner in Scottsdale get a chance to appeal?

In some cases. If the former owner never appealed the value or class, a new owner may file in court before December 15 of the year the taxes are levied. The usual administrative deadline is 60 days after the Notice of Value is mailed.

Last updated November 14, 2026.

Behind on Mesa property tax?
We buy Mesa houses as-is, and the title company pays unpaid tax from the proceeds.
Get My Cash Offer →

Who bills Mesa property tax

Mesa residents pay the Maricopa County Treasurer's Office, not City Hall. Valuation comes from the Maricopa County Assessor. Mesa doesn't assess or collect anything itself, yet its charge appears on the same statement as the county, school district, community college district and special districts.

Payment questions go to the Treasurer's customer service line, 602-506-8511. Value questions go to the Assessor, 602-506-3406. You can visit the Treasurer in person at 301 West Jefferson Street, Suite 100, Phoenix, between 8 a.m. and 5 p.m.

The city's share of the bill

Mesa levies no primary property tax and does levy a secondary one. Under Arizona's two-part system, that secondary tax repays voter-approved general obligation bonds for libraries, parks and recreation, public safety and transportation. The rate held steady for the three most recent years in the table.

Fiscal yearTaxable valueCity rate per $100 of valueCity levy
2025/26$5.2 billion$0.8582$44.3 million
2024/25$4.9 billion$0.8582$42.0 million
2023/24$4.5 billion$0.8582$38.8 million
2022/23$4.2 billion$0.9157$38.8 million
2021/22$4.0 billion$1.1319$45.2 million

A median-value Mesa home paid $159 of city secondary levy in 2025/26. Some parcels also sit in a Community Facility District, where bonds financed property development and the cost is assessed to the owners. If you aren't sure whether your parcel is inside one, the Treasurer can tell you, and the answer changes your bill.

Due dates and penalties

The city follows the county's schedule. Two installments are due, one on October 1 and one on March 1 (A.R.S. 42-18052), and each becomes delinquent at 5:00 p.m. on November 1 or May 1. Weekend and holiday cutoffs slide forward to the next business day, which gave the 2026 first half until 5 p.m. on Monday, November 2.

  • Pay all of the 2026 tax over $100 by December 31, 2026, and no interest applies.
  • Second-half money is due March 1, 2027.
  • May 1, 2027 lands on a Saturday, so lateness starts at 5:00 p.m. the next business day.
  • A bill of $100 or less is due whole on October 1 and goes late after December 31.

Interest on late tax is simple, 16% a year, counted from the delinquency date (A.R.S. 42-18053). Pay the full year by December 31, or have the delay traced to an office error, and it isn't charged. The Treasurer's calendar also schedules an advertising fee in January for delinquent taxes and an online lien auction in February.

Appealing a Mesa assessment

Your petition goes to the Maricopa County Assessor, and the clock is 60 days from the mailing of the Notice of Value. The notice arrives between January 1 and March 1. A.R.S. 42-16051 sets that window and treats a postmark as filing. Give your own figure for full cash value and the method behind it, for example a comparable property or a recent sale.

Only full cash value and legal classification can be appealed. Tax is figured on limited value, which is held to 5% growth a year unless the house itself changes. Values lag the market: they rest on sales from two to three years earlier, so the value used for fiscal 2025/26 came from mid-2022 to mid-2023 sales.

If the Assessor's reply leaves you unsatisfied, the State Board of Equalization hears an appeal filed within 25 days. Court is the last step, in Superior Court's tax division or small claims, by December 15 of the notice year or 60 days after an administrative decision. Small claims suits are for owner-occupied homes and property under $2 million. A rental that isn't the owner's primary residence belongs in tax court.

Selling a Mesa home: what buyers ask

Mesa counted 504,258 residents in 2020 and is estimated at 513,656 for 2025. Mesa Public Schools covers most of the city. The southern part is served by Gilbert Public Schools, the Higley Unified School District and the Queen Creek Unified School District, and a thin western strip belongs to Tempe districts. Buyers who compare schools will want to know your district, and it also shapes the school share of your bill.

Center Street is the east-west dividing line, and address numbering differs from Phoenix's, so verify yours before it goes on a deed or listing. Home ages range widely: the city grew from 16,790 residents in 1950 to 63,049 in 1970 and passed 500,000 by 2020.

Changes that raise your assessed value

A new room, a major addition or a switch in how the property is used can lift limited property value past the 5% cap. The Assessor then sends a Notice of Change, and you have 25 days to appeal to the State Board of Equalization. Save the permits for anything you built, since they show what was added and when. A buyer's agent may ask for them, and so might the Assessor.

Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

Tax due at closing

Think of the county bill as a payoff figure. The tax lien for the year attached on January 1 (A.R.S. 42-17153) and outranks most other liens, state liens and liens for other years excepted. The Treasurer can quote what is owed through your closing date. Send that number to the title company, which pays it from your proceeds. Interest on a delinquent half has been running since it went late.

Recording is a separate step. The deed and the affidavit of property value required by A.R.S. 11-1133 go to the Maricopa County Recorder, at $30 per document. Title companies normally handle the payoff and the recording together.

A simple order of work: look up your parcel on the Treasurer's site to see if either half is open, request the payoff, send it to title, then read the settlement statement for a tax line that matches. If a cash buyer closes quickly, less interest builds on a late half, although the balance still comes out of the sale at closing.

After closing, mail addressed to you may still arrive. Forward any tax bill to the new owner, and keep your closing statement as proof of what was paid and when, in case a question comes up later about which half belonged to whom.

Frequently asked questions

Does Mesa have its own property tax?

Only a secondary one. Mesa has no primary levy, and the secondary tax repays voter-approved bonds. The 2025/26 rate was $0.8582 per $100 of value, which was $159 for a median-value home.

Where do I pay Mesa property tax?

Pay the Maricopa County Treasurer, who collects for Mesa along with the county, schools and special districts. You can pay on the Treasurer's website, by calling 602-506-8511, or at 301 West Jefferson Street, Suite 100, Phoenix.

When did the 2026 first-half Mesa property tax go delinquent?

At 5:00 p.m. on Monday, November 2, 2026, since November 1 was a Sunday. Pay the full year by December 31, 2026 to avoid interest. The second half is due March 1, 2027.

How long do I have to contest my Mesa property value?

Sixty days, counted from the day the Maricopa County Assessor mailed your Notice of Value. Use the Petition for Review of Real Property Valuation. If you appeal further, the State Board of Equalization wants it within 25 days of the Assessor's decision.

Can I sell a Mesa house that still owes property tax?

Yes. At closing the title company takes the lien amount out of your proceeds. Ask the Treasurer for a payoff dated to closing, because overdue amounts accrue 16% a year.
